lesson.text: Quick memory: what does empathy mean? (Imagining how someone else feels.) Imagine being picked on again and again. Today: what bullying is, and how to stand up to it safely.
Bullying is when someone hurts another person on purpose, again and again, and the person finds it hard to stop it. A one-off argument between friends is not bullying, but it still needs sorting out.

It can be hitting or pushing, calling names, or leaving someone out on purpose. It can be spreading stories, or being unkind online in messages, games or photos. Bullying is never the fault of the person picked on.
If it happens to you: tell a grown-up you trust, like a parent or a teacher, and keep telling until it stops. Stay near friends. You deserve to feel safe.
Online: do not reply. Save what was sent (a grown-up can help you take a screenshot). Then block and report the person, and tell a grown-up you trust.
If you see it, be an upstander, not a bystander: don't join in or laugh, stay with the person being picked on, and tell a grown-up. Never put yourself in danger.
Worked example: in a game chat, someone keeps calling Tilly names. Zara does not reply to them. She messages Tilly, 'That's not OK, I'm with you,' and they tell a grown-up together, who reports it.

picture.name: Tilly
messages: That's not OK. I'm with you.

lesson.text: Try it in the world: in the game, tap another player's name to find REPORT and BLOCK. Put up a sign at your base: 'Here everyone is welcome.' Next: smart spending.

exercises.hint: Think of two things: on purpose, and again and again.
choices: hurting someone on purpose, again and again
exercises.explain: Bullying is hurting someone on purpose, again and again, when it is hard for them to stop it.

exercises.prompt: Bullying is the fault of the person being picked on.
exercises.hint: Does anyone deserve to be hurt?
exercises.explain: False: bullying is never the fault of the person picked on.

exercises.prompt: Someone sends you unkind messages online. What should you NOT do?
exercises.hint: Which choice could make it worse?
exercises.explain: Don't reply. Save it, block and report, and tell a grown-up you trust.

exercises.prompt: Who should you tell if you are being bullied?
exercises.hint: Who can help to make it stop?
exercises.explain: Tell a grown-up you trust, like a parent or a teacher, and keep telling until it stops.

exercises.prompt: Sort these: bullying, or not bullying?
items: leaving someone out on purpose, again and again
exercises.hint: Is it on purpose, and again and again?
exercises.explain: Bullying: daily name-calling, leaving someone out again and again, repeated unkind messages. Not bullying: one argument, one 'not today', or losing a race.

exercises.prompt: Put the steps for dealing with unkind messages in order.
exercises.hint: Stop it growing first, then keep the evidence.
exercises.explain: Don't reply, save the messages, block and report the person, and tell a grown-up you trust.

exercises.prompt: Match each kind of bullying to an example.
exercises.explain: Physical: pushing. Name-calling: calling names. Leaving out: never letting someone join. Online: unkind messages.

exercises.hint: The opposite of a bystander, who just watches.
choices: someone who helps safely when they see bullying
someone who stands up all day
exercises.explain: An upstander helps safely: stays with the person, doesn't join in, and tells a grown-up.

exercises.prompt: A one-off argument between friends is bullying.
exercises.hint: Is it on purpose, again and again?
exercises.explain: False: a one-off argument is not bullying, but it still needs sorting out kindly.

exercises.prompt: You see an older child picking on a younger one in the park. What is the safest way to help?
exercises.hint: Help, but never put yourself in danger.
exercises.explain: Get a grown-up straight away. Fighting could hurt you, and sharing films makes it worse.

exercises.prompt: Why save unkind messages before blocking?
exercises.hint: What does a grown-up need in order to help?
choices: a grown-up can see what happened and report it
to read them again for fun
exercises.explain: Saved messages show what happened, so a grown-up can report it and get it stopped.

exercises.prompt: Laughing along with bullying can make it worse.
exercises.hint: What does the bully see when others laugh?
exercises.explain: True: laughing shows the bully that others are joining in. Upstanders don't laugh.

exercises.prompt: Zara messaged Tilly: 'That's not OK, I'm with you.' How might Tilly feel?
exercises.explain: Knowing someone is on her side helps Tilly feel less alone, and braver about getting help.

exercises.prompt: Bram tells a teacher, but the name-calling goes on. What should he do?
exercises.hint: Remember: keep telling until it stops.
choices: keep telling, or tell another grown-up
exercises.explain: Keep telling: another teacher, a parent or another grown-up. He deserves to feel safe.

exercises.prompt: Sort what an upstander does and doesn't do.
items: stays with the person picked on
exercises.hint: An upstander helps safely and never adds to the hurt.
exercises.explain: An upstander stays with the person, tells a grown-up and safely says 'that's not OK'. They never laugh along, join in or share films, which all make it worse.

exercises.prompt: Match each situation to the best next step.
items: a friend is left out every day
exercises.hint: Think about online, in person, being left out, and when it goes on.
exercises.explain: Unkind messages: save them, block, report and tell a grown-up. Someone pushed: get a grown-up straight away. A friend left out: invite them to join you. If it goes on: keep telling until it stops.
